messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 68
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Unemployed
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 41

Mrs. A. is a 68-year-old woman of Ghanaian descent who lives with her second husband in a quiet suburban apartment. She speaks softly, often pausing to look down at her hands folded in her lap. When she begins to tell her story, her voice drops barely above a whisper, as if she is afraid someone might overhear.

She met her first husband in Accra when she was twenty-three. He was charming, attentive, and her family approved. The first time he hit her was three months after the wedding. She remembers the shock more than the pain—the way his face twisted, the sound of her own head hitting the kitchen wall. He apologized afterward, brought her flowers, swore it would never happen again. She believed him. Over the next twelve years, the beatings came in cycles—weeks of tension, an explosion, then remorse and promises. She learned to read the signs: the clench of his jaw, the sudden silence, the way he would come home later than usual. She would send the children to her mother’s house. She would try to stay out of his way.

The worst night came during a thunderstorm. He accused her of speaking to a neighbor. She does not remember the blows, only waking up on the bathroom floor with blood in her mouth and her left arm twisted beneath her. That was the night she decided to leave. She gathered her two children, took only a small bag, and went to her sister’s house. The next week she filed for divorce. She never pressed charges. In Ghana, it was still a private matter.

She came to the United States at forty-two, sponsored by a church group. She worked as a home health aide for fifteen years, caring for elderly patients. She was good at it—patient, gentle, attentive. But she never felt safe. She watched every man who entered a room, always noting the exits. She avoided crowds, and if a male coworker raised his voice in laughter, her heart would hammer so hard she had to excuse herself to the bathroom. She told herself it was just nerves.

When she retired at sixty-five, the structure of work disappeared, and the memories grew louder. Now she spends most of her time at home. She cleans, she cooks, she watches television. Her current husband, a retired postal worker she met eight years ago, is a kind man. He never raises his voice. He asks gently if she wants to go for a walk. She often says no. She is afraid of being seen, of running into someone who might remind her. She does not tell him why she flinches when he touches her shoulder from behind. She does not tell him about the nightmares—the same one, over and over: she is back in that kitchen, and the storm is outside, and she cannot move her legs.

She blames herself. She believes she should have left sooner, that she was weak, that she failed her children. When her daughter calls, she puts on a cheerful voice, but afterward she sits in the dark for an hour. She has stopped visiting the grocery store on weekends; the noise, the movement, the men—it all feels too much. Last month, a man in a baseball cap accidentally bumped into her at the pharmacy, and she burst into tears. Her husband had to bring her home.

She agreed to come to therapy after that episode. She sits in the chair across from me, her posture rigid, her eyes scanning the room. She says she does not know why she is still so afraid. She thought she had left it all behind in Accra.
